rv.q: Perhaps everyone was rather too consumed with cementing Berg's likability, which was certainly her greatest asset and something the very charming Gold has down cold, but plays (and actors of Gold's quality) need complex, imperfect characters who wrestle with their demons and their fellow humans.
Jones has proven again and again that he’s a director with a gift for addressing social issues with a deft hand that laces comedy and tragedy together, with nary a seam.
James Sherman’s "The First Lady of Television" is astounding.
Ms. Gold is simply wonderful in her consistent, charming take on a woman much more accomplished than people knew.
This drama, laced with humor, isn’t just an entertaining historical play.
I was genuinely delighted by how thoroughly I enjoyed this production, far exceeding my expectations and leaving a lasting impression.
The actress inhabits Berg so effectively, so authentically it’s hard to imagine anyone else playing the part.
Let me alert you that this is more than a comedy; it’s a drama about the rise of McCarthyism in mid-century America and its effect on artists, actors and TV shows.
Like all great theatre, The First Lady of Television entertains, enlightens, and inspires.
The history is worth coming to see.

cn.t: Critics praise this world premiere for its compelling dramatization of sitcom pioneer Gertrude Berg's story, highlighting strong performances and timely themes about McCarthyism and artistic integrity in 1950s television.
